title: Jackson Lake Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Jackson Lake wells have a 54-foot median depth. See local yields, water levels, permits, risks, and drilling costs.
intro_html:
Buying land near Jackson Lake means looking closely at the well records, not relying on a general county average. Within 5 miles of Jackson Lake, Colorado DWR records show 594 permitted wells, with 402 recorded as constructed. Of those, 366 report a total depth, 78 report a pump yield, and 36 report a static water level.

This area is plains country near Orchard and Weldona, with alluvium and plains sedimentary rock rather than a uniform hard-rock setting. The records suggest many relatively shallow wells, but the spread in reported production and water levels still matters when pricing a property, planning a septic system, or requesting a drilling bid.

sections.heading: Jackson Lake well depth: usually shallow, but not guaranteed
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Jackson Lake is 54 feet. The middle half of wells falls from 40 to 124 feet, and the 90th percentile is 163 feet. About 70% of wells are under 100 feet, while 29% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Only 1% are between 300 and 600 feet, with no recorded wells at 600 feet or more.

That distribution gives a driller a useful starting point, not a guarantee. Local alluvium and plains sedimentary rock can change quickly across a parcel. A bid based on the 54-foot median may be reasonable for a straightforward site, but buyers should ask what happens if the hole reaches the upper part of the local range, or if casing, grout, access, and difficult ground add work.

sections.heading: How much water do Jackson Lake wells produce?
sections.html:
Reported yields are strong in this record set, but the sample is limited to 78 wells that report a pump yield. The median is 65.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half ranges from 15.0 to 987.5 gallons per minute. The records show 88% producing 15 or more gallons per minute, 10% between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 1% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

These figures include domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells, so they do not predict a household well by themselves. Pump tests, well construction, storage, and the permitted use matter. Do not assume an irrigation result applies to a domestic permit, and confirm the legal water use with Colorado DWR before closing.

sections.heading: Water levels near Jackson Lake and the recent change
sections.html:
Only 36 wells report a static water level, so the water-level picture is narrower than the depth picture. The median depth to static water is 18 feet, with the middle half from 13 to 70 feet below ground surface. That is useful for estimating casing, trenching, and pumping conditions, but it is not a guarantee for an untested parcel.

The decade figures show a higher measured water level depth in newer records: the median was 15 feet below surface in the 2010s and 37 feet in the 2020s. That difference suggests a possible decline in measured water levels, but the small reporting set, different locations, and well uses make it unsafe to call the entire Jackson Lake area a uniformly dropping water table. Get a current static measurement when evaluating a specific well.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Jackson Lake, and when?
sections.html:
Permit activity stretches across the area’s history. Records list 40 permits in the 1950s, 45 in the 1960s, 59 in the 1970s, 21 in the 1980s, 35 in the 1990s, 72 in the 2000s, 77 in the 2010s, and 44 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. That history shows continued drilling near the lake, Orchard, and Weldona rather than a one-time development pattern.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 81 wells, Wiggins Irrigation & Agri Serv (Segelke, Virgil A) with 40, and Canfield Drilling Company (Canfield, Harold E) with 38. Treat the list as permit-history context, not a current recommendation or a promise of availability.

sections.heading: What drilling a Jackson Lake well may cost
sections.html:
For this plains setting, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $35 to $55 per foot. At the local median depth of 54 feet, the drilled hole works out to about $1,900 to $3,000. That is only the hole. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $7,900 to $15,000.

Ask every driller what is included. A low drilling number may exclude casing, grout, development, pump sizing, power work, or long access across a lot. The median depth is shallow, but the deepest recorded well is 590 feet, so a quote should explain the additional-foot rate and what happens if the target water-bearing material is not reached. Permitting and water-right requirements are separate questions from construction cost.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying near the lake
sections.html:
The records name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 493 wells, Quaternary Alluvium for 31, and Alluvial aquifers for 28. They also show Denver Basin aquifer wells at 33% of the mapped records. Aquifer labels can vary by permit and do not replace a site-specific review. Fractured material can be unpredictable, while alluvial conditions can affect water quality, casing, and well construction.

Environmental screening deserves attention. The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 44 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, with 0 historic mine features and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test existing well water for the uses and local concerns that apply to the property. Also check septic setbacks, drainfield soil, flood or irrigation impacts, and whether the lot can support the proposed home before committing to a well location.

sections.heading: A practical Jackson Lake lot-buying plan
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, not just the nearest well on a map. Pull the DWR permit, construction report, pump information, and water-quality history for the property and nearby wells. Compare depth, static level, aquifer description, permitted use, and construction details. The area includes domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells, so similar distance does not mean similar performance.

For a new build, confirm the well permit and water-use rules before finalizing plans. Exempt household-use wells still have defined limits, including the 35 gallons-per-minute exempt-well pumping limit, and an augmentation plan may be necessary in an over-appropriated basin. Have a driller evaluate access, casing and grout, pump setting, trench route, and backup locations. In a purchase contract, preserve time for well testing, water testing, septic review, and a cost check based on the actual site.

faq.q: How deep are wells near Jackson Lake, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth is 54 feet. The middle half runs from 40 to 124 feet, and 70% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. Depth still varies by parcel and formation. The deepest recorded well in the data is 590 feet, so a local median should guide a bid, not guarantee the final depth.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well near Jackson Lake?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35 to $55 per foot. At the 54-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $1,900 to $3,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is about $7,900 to $15,000. Confirm what each bid includes and the additional-foot rate.

faq.q: How much water do wells near Jackson Lake produce?
faq.a: Among the 78 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 65.0 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 987.5 gallons per minute, and 88% report at least 15 gallons per minute. These records include different uses, so a domestic buyer should require a site-specific pump test.

faq.q: Is well water near Jackson Lake safe to drink?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that water is safe for drinking. Within about 10 miles, mapping shows 44 PFAS sampling or contamination sites. That calls for testing the specific well, especially when buying an existing home. Review construction and water-quality records, then use a qualified laboratory for drinking-water testing before relying on the supply.

faq.q: Are Jackson Lake wells getting deeper or losing water?
faq.a: The reported median static water level was 15 feet below surface in the 2010s and 37 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper measured water levels in newer records, but only 36 wells report static levels. Different wells and uses can affect the comparison, so obtain a current measurement for the property rather than treating the series as conclusive.
